strengths: PST addresses a meaningful problem in language-conditioned image generation: gender stereotypes when depicting multiple people together. The systematic occupation pairings, reversed spatial orders, and organizational-role contrasts provide a useful evaluation framework.

The human annotation protocol uses three annotators and reports strong agreement (Fleiss’ kappa 0.88–0.92). Explicit annotation instructions and detailed occupation-level results support the descriptive finding that DALL-E-3 produces stereotyped associations under PST.

FairCritic is a plausible mitigation approach. The reported aggregate SS reductions—from 47.38 to 2.00 for occupations and 18.98 to 5.09 for organizational power—provide promising preliminary evidence.
weaknesses: The central fairness conclusion exceeds what the metric establishes. SS is a signed average, so opposing biases can cancel. Table 1 illustrates this directly: female SS of 50 and male SS of −30 produce an overall score of 10 in the single-person setting. Reporting male/female aggregates only partially addresses cancellation; substantial differences between occupations can remain hidden. Without occupation-level post-mitigation distributions and uncertainty estimates, an aggregate score near zero does not establish 'near-perfect fairness.'

The headline percentage of 'biased images' lacks an appropriate reference point. Under independent, equally probable binary gender assignments, 75% of two-person images would satisfy PST(Any), because at least one person would match an occupational stereotype. Consequently, the reported 74.3% is not independently evidence of distributional bias. The high PST(Both) rate and occupation-level distributions remain informative, but the manuscript conflates stereotype-conforming individual samples with biased generation distributions.

FairCritic is insufficiently specified for reproduction. Section 5.1 identifies the critic model and one-loop limit but omits exact critic instructions, the number and selection of images supplied to each decision, how feedback is incorporated, and clear evaluation sample counts. The conflicting totals of 944 and 1,952 prompts also need reconciliation. These omissions concern a central contribution, rather than optional implementation details.

The mitigation comparison does not establish FairCritic’s claimed superiority. Table 2 evaluates the intervention baseline on the five most biased occupations per gender, whereas Table 1 reports FairCritic over the full occupation set. These scores are not directly comparable. Matched prompts and generation budgets, together with an ablation comparing adaptive criticism against fixed fairness guidance, are needed to identify the benefit of the critic.

The single-person baseline contains only three images per identity, making occupation-level amplification estimates and selected qualitative contrasts unstable. No confidence intervals or statistical uncertainty analysis accompany these claims. Anti-stereotypical examples also do not establish that the underlying single-person distribution is fair. Substantive evaluation covers only DALL-E-3, limiting conclusions about T2I systems generally.

The annotation procedure assumes that generated people occupy the requested positions and fulfill the requested roles, without reporting a systematic check of this correspondence. Handling of 'Cannot Identify' responses and generation failures is unclear. Prompt fidelity should also be measured after mitigation: gender balance alone cannot demonstrate successful generation of the requested occupational or power relationship. Together with the metric and reproducibility issues, these concerns warrant revision before a positive Findings recommendation.
